_what: The measured orthographic-depth axis the programme's independent variable is defined on. Every value is BORROWED from a published measurement, never re-derived, because re-deriving it with a different model would produce a different instrument and the numbers would not be comparable (global rule 19, instrument unity).

instrument.metric: orthographic transparency as mutual compressibility between orthographic and phonological strings
instrument.reference: Torres & Futrell, 'Clarifying orthography: Orthographic transparency as compressibility', arXiv 2505.13657 (May 2025)
instrument.estimated_by: prequential code-lengths from neural sequence models, fitted per language
instrument.why_borrowed_rather_than_recomputed: The metric's value depends on the sequence model that estimates it. Re-fitting with our own model would place the numbers on a different scale from the published ones and from the 22 languages already measured, which is exactly the failure rule 19 exists to prevent.
instrument.direction: the source reports BOTH orthography-to-phonology and phonology-to-orthography mappings; the phonology-to-orthography direction is the production/spelling direction this programme's corpora live in
instrument.verification_status: BORROWED. Values transcribed from the source's between-language table (its Table 1), which reports differences from a reference language. NOT independently re-measured here.

scale.anchor: spa (Spanish) = 0.0, the most transparent language in the source's set
scale.unit: transparency difference in the source's metric; negative = LESS transparent (deeper)
scale.how_derived: the source's Table 1 gives pairwise differences; the column for Spanish was read as each language's distance from the transparent end
scale.limitation: derived from a difference table rather than from absolute values, so the spacing is exact but the zero point is the source's reference language rather than an absolute scale

segmental_cluster.reading: The twenty segmental languages occupy a range of only 0.216. Depth differences inside this cluster are SMALL, so a comparison of two segmental languages tests a small effect that may sit near the noise floor.

logographic_outliers.reading: The two non-segmental languages sit far outside the cluster. The large, robust contrast available to this programme is cluster versus outlier, not one segmental language versus another.

structure.consequence_for_the_design: The axis's SHAPE is carried by the logographic arm, and within-cluster variation can only be tested weakly. This is why the primary contrast is English against Chinese and why the generator's twelve languages test within-cluster variation rather than the axis.

covered_by_published_values.reading: All seven sit inside the compressed segmental cluster, spanning 0.112. The generator therefore spans within-cluster variation, NOT the axis.

not_covered.status: No published value under this instrument. They must NOT be filled in with a locally fitted model, because that would put two instruments' numbers on one table. Either they stay off the axis, or the source's own fitting procedure is reproduced exactly.

jpn.note: the kanji-conversion channel exercises the logographic end of this value, not the syllabic end; see docs/THEORETICAL_ANCHOR.md

corrections_this_measurement_forced: The programme had assumed Russian, Hindi and Tamil were 'shallow'. Measured, Russian (-0.185) and Hindi (-0.175) are among the DEEPEST of the segmental set. The assumption was wrong.

The programme treated Turkish as a candidate shallow extreme. Measured, Turkish (-0.100) sits mid-cluster; the true transparent extreme is Spanish (0.000), then Italian, Czech and Polish. If a shallow arm is added, Spanish is the theoretically strongest choice, not Turkish.
Both corrections are the reason the axis was measured rather than asserted.
